reconcile.connective: Defenders distinguish God's overruling of evil from God's authoring of it: He permits the lying spirit and the strong delusion as a righteous judgment, but does not Himself lie.

discrepancy.connective: Thomas Paine presses the sharpest objection: he reads 1 Kings 22, where God personally commissions a lying spirit, as proof that Scripture's own God authorizes deception, calling it "another blasphemous story of God."

excerpts.excerpt_text: I the Lord have deceived that prophet—not directly, but through Satan and his ministers; not merely permissively, but by overruling their evil to serve the purposes of His righteous judgment, to be a touchstone to separate the precious from the vile, and to "prove" His people … Evil comes not from God, though God overrules it to serve His will …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly answers the 'God deceives' charge on Ezekiel 14:9 by drawing the precise distinction the contradiction turns on — God overrules evil for judgment but does not originate the lie. Single strongest reconcile voice; parity-capped to the discrepancy pole's one named-skeptic count.

pd_work.resource: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832), on 1 Kings 22:23 and Ezekiel 14:9
pd_work.author: Adam Clarke
pd_work.note: Clarke treats this passage directly, arguing the Scripture 'repeatedly represent[s] God as doing what, in the course of his providence, he only permits or suffers to be done' — the permission-not-authorship harmonization keyed to these verses.
